title: Busy Tricking During the Do Now
author: Craig Barton
summary: Barton takes up Adam Boxer's term 'busy tricking' - students giving the outward impression of working while taking actions to avoid thinking - and shows how it hides in the Do Now. His centrepiece is a lesson observation in which a student spent the whole five minutes slowly copying the date, title and question topics, then copied the teacher's answers in green pen, producing a book that looked exemplary despite no thinking having taken place. He argues the behaviour is rife but hard to spot because, unlike chatting or refusal, it looks like work from the front of the room. He proposes four countermeasures: make the purpose of the Do Now explicit to students, circulate purposefully instead of doing admin at the front, require mass participation with mini-whiteboards so blank boards are visible, and for low-attention classes present Do Now questions one at a time with a show-me after each. The piece extends his previous week's argument about copying into a question of classroom routine and vigilance.
points: Busy tricking is defined as disguised off-task behaviour - slow copying of dates, titles or questions - that evades detection because from a distance it looks like working.
Barton's observed example shows a student producing a flawless-looking Do Now entirely through copying, illustrating how book policies can mask a total absence of thinking.
Students' own accounts of the Do Now's purpose ('to keep us busy while Sir does the register') suggest the purpose of retrieval practice is rarely communicated to them.
Mass participation via mini-whiteboards acts as a check for effort as well as understanding, changing the incentive so that thinking becomes preferable to being put on the spot.
For classes prone to busy tricking, he recommends doing admin first and then running Do Now questions one at a time with whole-class responses.
quotes: Busy tricking is when students give the outward impression that they are engaging with work, but in reality, they are taking actions to avoid thinking. Slowly copying down the date, title and lesson objectives are classic busy tricking behaviours at the start of a lesson when the Do Now is also on the board.
Quite simply, the student learned very little, if anything, during the Do Now. How could she have, when she hadn’t needed to engage in any thought?
Unlike the teacher, who has lots of other things to think about, I am able to choose to focus my attention on specific things at any given time. And believe me, busy tricking is rife.

If I ask a student - as I regularly do - why they are doing the Do Now, they often reply along the line of: “to keep us busy while Sir does the register”, or “dunno”. If students understand the purpose of what they are doing, they are more likely to buy into it.

Even if they regularly glance up at the students to check that they are working, they are unlikely to pick up on busy tricking because from a distance busy tricking looks like working. Purposefully circulating the room several times during the Do Now gives you a more reliable sense of what your students are actually engaging in.

Now the teacher has both a check for understanding as well as a check for effort. Anyone holding up a blank board is the first to be questioned. Students quickly realise that spending time thinking during the Do Now is preferable to being put on the spot, and thus the incentive to opt out diminishes.
